patterns: why did my password leak from phishing
entries.answer: Phishing is a message that impersonates something trusted to get a person to reveal a password or click a link. It works because it attacks the person rather than the software, which is why a strong password alone does not help. The reliable defence is to check the actual sender and the actual destination rather than what the message claims, and to use a password manager that will not autofill on the wrong domain.

entries.answer: Malware is any software written to do something the user did not intend, and the categories differ by what they do rather than how they spread. Viruses attach to files, worms spread on their own, trojans look legitimate, ransomware encrypts and demands payment, and spyware quietly records. The defence is layered, and the single most effective layer is not running what you did not deliberately install.

patterns: how do i prevent sql injection
entries.answer: SQL injection is a defect where input from a user is pasted into a database query instead of being passed as data, so the input can change the meaning of the statement. The fix is not escaping, which is easy to get subtly wrong, but parameterised queries, where the database treats the input as a value no matter what it contains. It is still common because string-concatenated SQL is quick to write and looks correct.

patterns: what is a content security policy
entries.answer: Cross-site scripting is a defect where user input is inserted into a page as markup rather than as text, so the browser runs it. The standard defence is output encoding matched to context, since escaping for HTML is not the same as escaping for a script block or an attribute. A content security policy is the second layer, because it limits what a page is allowed to execute even if something slips through.

entries.answer: Two-factor authentication requires a second piece of evidence beyond the password, and the types are not equal in strength. Something you know is the password, something you have is a code from your phone, and something you are is a fingerprint. The second is much stronger than the first because the phone cannot be phished into revealing it, which is why a rotating app code beats an SMS code.

entries.answer: A hash turns input into a fixed-length fingerprint, and unlike encryption it cannot be reversed, which is exactly why passwords are stored as hashes. Salting means giving every user a different random value before hashing, so two people with the same password do not produce the same stored value and precomputed tables become useless. Deliberately slow algorithms such as bcrypt or argon2 are used for passwords, because speed helps an attacker and not a defender.

patterns: how long should a password be
entries.answer: Password strength is mostly about length rather than the mixture of character types, and the current guidance is to prefer several unrelated words over a short scrambled string. A long passphrase survives a brute-force attempt that a complex short password does not, because length multiplies the work. Reuse is the actual risk, since one breached site is enough to attack every account sharing that password, which is why a unique password per site matters more than a strong one reused.

patterns: how to make a strong password
entries.answer: A long password beats a complicated short one - length matters more than symbols, and a four-word phrase is both stronger and easier to remember. Use a different one everywhere, because breaches are reused. Turn on two-factor authentication wherever it is offered, and prefer an authenticator app or a hardware key over SMS. Never act on an unexpected link: go to the site yourself instead.
